svg.title: OSPF LSA types with generator, flooding scope, and the design consequence of each
svg.desc: Seven rows. Type 1 Router LSA, generated by every router, scoped to the area, describes who each router is connected to and at what cost, so an interface flap produces a new LSA. Type 2 Network LSA, generated by the DR, scoped to the area, describes the set of routers on a broadcast segment. Type 3 Summary LSA, generated by the ABR, crosses areas, and is where inter-area summarization happens. Type 4 Summary ASBR LSA, generated by the ABR, tells other areas where the ASBR is. Type 5 AS External LSA, generated by the ASBR, floods the whole AS except stub areas, and is what redistribution produces. Type 7 NSSA External LSA lets a stub-like area import external routes and is converted to Type 5 by the ABR. Types 9 to 11 are opaque LSAs carrying extensions such as MPLS-TE, graceful restart and segment routing. A side note explains why Type 4 exists: Type 5 carries only the ASBR router ID, so other areas need a reachable address for it.
svg.text: Seven LSA types, and the one thing each is responsible for
Learn them as “who generates it, how far does it travel” — the design follows from the scope
“who I am connected to, at what cost” — a flapping interface generates a new one each time
the set of routers on a broadcast segment — point-to-point links never produce one
this is where inter-area summarization happens — area X range lives here
tells other areas where the ASBR is, so Type 5 can be resolved
redistribution produces these — the LSA that turns a mistake into a network-wide event
lets a stub-like area import external routes; the ABR translates it back to Type 5
carries extensions: MPLS-TE, graceful restart, segment routing
Why Type 4 exists (the one most people never learn): Type 5 contains only the ASBR's router ID. Routers in other areas
need a reachable address to compute “how do I get to that ASBR”, so the ABR writes a location sheet on its behalf. Stub areas need neither.
Practical filter for the design review: for each LSA type, ask who generates it and how far it travels. If you cannot name both, the area design is not finished.
